planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Albiflora offers soft, creamy-white single flowers instead of the species' typical yellow, on the same bright green, arching, bamboo-like canes.

directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Albiflora is a white-flowered sport of Japanese kerria, opening ivory to creamy-white, single, wild-rose-like blooms with soft butter-yellow centers in mid to late spring, a gentler alternative to the species' bright gold flush. The bright green, slender, cane-like stems stay vividly green through winter after leaf drop, giving the shrub a second season of interest even when bare. It tolerates dry shade better than most flowering shrubs and suckers moderately to form a colony over time; thin out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering each year to keep growth open and floriferous.

common_name: Spring Glory Forsythia (Pale Gold Early Spring Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Spring Glory flowers most heavily in full sun and tolerates part shade with a lighter bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Spring Glory is an older, reliable forsythia selection prized for its paler, soft primrose-yellow flowers, a gentler contrast to the electric gold of many modern cultivars, produced in such profusion along the arching branches that the entire shrub disappears under bloom before the forest-green foliage emerges. It forms a large, upright, rounded shrub with slightly arching branches and needs room to reach its mature size. Prune immediately after flowering only, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth soon after bloom; avoid shearing, which removes flower buds and produces a stubby, sparse-blooming plant.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Fiesta is grown chiefly for its variegated foliage, so give it full sun to preserve the strongest leaf color, and expect a lighter flower display than solid-green cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Fiesta arose as a sport of 'Lynwood Gold' and is grown primarily for its strikingly variegated foliage, each leaf marked with a rich green center broadly bordered in creamy yellow, giving the compact mound season-long color long after the deep yellow, comparatively sparse early-spring flowers on reddish stems have faded. It stays noticeably smaller and denser than typical border forsythia, making it useful as a specimen or accent rather than a hedge. Watch for any shoots that revert to solid green and remove them at the base promptly, since reverted growth is more vigorous and will overtake the variegated wood if left unchecked.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this dwarf selection is easy to grow and tolerates a wide range of soils.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Bronx forsythia is a true dwarf, originating from a Japanese seed source grown at the Bronx Botanical Garden in 1939, forming a low, flat, spreading mound only about a foot tall with distinctive greenish stems and chambered pith. In early to mid-spring it is dotted with small, pale primrose-yellow flowers, a subtler and shorter display than full-size border forsythias but still a welcome early color note. Its low, spreading habit makes it useful as a groundcover, low border edge, or cascading accent over a wall, and it needs only occasional thinning to stay tidy since it rarely outgrows its allotted space.

common_name: Amethyst Snowberry (Doorenbos Coralberry with Deep Pink Berries)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall into average, well-drained soil in sun to part shade.

directions: Bred from Symphoricarpos x doorenbosii crosses developed in the Netherlands, 'Amethyst' is grown chiefly for its abundant, vividly colored, deep purple-pink berries that ripen in dense clusters in early fall and persist into winter, well above the merely white or pale berries of the species types. The small, greenish-white early-summer flowers are ornamentally insignificant, but they are followed by this outstanding fruit display valued for cutting as well as garden interest. It tolerates poor, rocky, or clay soils, dry shade, and root competition beneath established trees, and spreads slowly by suckers to form a loose thicket. Cut back hard every few years to renew flowering and fruiting wood and keep the colony from becoming twiggy.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Abbotswood is one of the best white-flowered selections and tolerates clay and alkaline soils.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun. Abbotswood is widely regarded as the best pure-white-flowered shrubby cinquefoil, producing masses of clean white, single, wild-rose-like blooms roughly 1.5 inches across from late spring until the first hard frosts, set against neat, fine-textured, blue-green foliage on a compact, mounded frame. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and tolerates clay, alkaline soil, drought once established, and salt spray, making it dependable for exposed sites and cold-climate gardens. Prune out a portion of the oldest stems at the base every few years to maintain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Goldfinger holds its deep gold flower color better than paler yellow cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun. Goldfinger produces an exceptionally heavy, near-continuous flush of deep golden-yellow flowers from late spring through fall against dark green, fine-textured foliage, giving noticeably richer color than many older yellow-flowered cultivars. Its dense, rounded habit and heavy bloom make it a reliable choice for low hedges, foundation plantings, and mixed shrub borders in cold climates. It tolerates clay, alkaline soil, and drought once established; prune out a portion of the oldest stems at the base every few years to keep the plant vigorous and well-flowered.

common_name: Pink Beauty Potentilla (Semi-Double Pink Shrubby Cinquefoil)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; flower color holds truest pink where summers are cool.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun, with light afternoon shade in hot-summer climates to preserve flower color. Pink Beauty bears semi-double, clear pink flowers from late spring to frost on a compact, mounded shrub with fine, blue-green foliage, one of the few reliably pink-toned selections in a genus dominated by yellow and white. Bloom color is strongest in cool weather and fades toward pale pink or cream during hot spells, a normal seasonal shift rather than a sign of stress. It tolerates clay and alkaline soils and drought once established; prune out a portion of the oldest stems at the base every few years to renew flowering wood.

common_name: Primrose Beauty Potentilla (Pale Yellow Silver-Leaved Shrubby Cinquefoil)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Primrose Beauty's silvery foliage is a standout feature even before bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun. Primrose Beauty pairs soft, pale primrose-yellow single flowers with striking blue-gray, silky-haired foliage, a two-season combination of bloom and foliage texture that sets it apart from greener-leaved cinquefoils. It blooms from June to frost on a broad, mounded shrub and tolerates clay, alkaline soil, and drought once established, remaining one of the most weather-resilient of the shrubby cinquefoils. Prune out a portion of the oldest stems at the base every few years to maintain vigorous flowering and a tidy mounded form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from cuttings in fall to allow root establishment through the rainy season, into well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; established plants need little to no summer water.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun and water only to establish, since summer irrigation on settled soil is the leading cause of root rot in this drought-adapted hybrid. Concha is a dense, arching, evergreen shrub bred from Ceanothus impressus and Ceanothus papillosus parentage, producing an exceptionally heavy late-spring display of deep cobalt-blue flower clusters set against small, dark, leathery leaves that gives it a reputation as one of the showiest blue-flowered ceanothus for garden use. It is more tolerant of occasional summer water and average garden conditions than many wild ceanothus species, making it a more forgiving choice for mixed borders as well as dry gardens. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since old bare wood does not reliably resprout.

common_name: Dark Star Ceanothus (Fragrant Cobalt-Blue California Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from cuttings in fall to allow root establishment through the rainy season, into well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; established plants need little to no summer water and resent soggy soil.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun and water only to establish; this coastal California hybrid resents summer irrigation once settled and is prone to root rot in soggy conditions. Dark Star forms a compact, vase-shaped evergreen shrub with rough-textured, tiny, dark green leaves, smothered from late winter into early spring in dense, fragrant clusters of intensely saturated cobalt to indigo-blue flowers that are among the darkest of any ceanothus in cultivation. Its wider-than-tall habit makes it useful as a large-scale groundcover on slopes as well as a specimen shrub, and it draws heavy pollinator activity in bloom. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since old bare wood does not reliably resprout.
